My family has farmed this same land in Quzhou for generations. I learned from my father and have been doing this for 25 years, so I know this ground. With 7 mouths to feed and some family members working in town, I need reliable harvests, not experiments. The wheat-maize rotation is what works here on the North China Plain — I have no reason to change it.

For wheat, I'll plant all 8 mu in October after the summer maize comes off. I've been buying improved certified seed from the county seed station for several years now — yields are better than the old varieties and the extension station recommends them. I apply compound fertilizer at planting and come back with urea at green-up in spring. That's how I've always done it. For irrigation, I'll run the pump about 4 times: before sowing to get good germination, winter water before the freeze, green-up in spring, and jointing. If it rains well at heading I might skip that last one. I'll spray herbicide once in winter and a fungicide at heading because powdery mildew comes every year. I rotary till after maize harvest to break up the stubble and smooth the seedbed.

For maize, I plant right after the wheat comes off in June — no time to waste. I use hybrid seed, same as everyone in the village. I don't deep plow between the two crops, just direct sow into the stubble. Summer rains usually carry the maize, but I'll irrigate at planting if the soil is dry and once more if August gets dry before tasseling. I top-dress with urea around knee height. I'll spray herbicide once early on and watch for corn borer — usually one more spray is enough.

decision.reasoning_summary: As an experienced farmer in Quzhou with 25 years on the same 8 mu of North China Plain land, I follow the established wheat-maize double-cropping rotation my father taught me, using improved wheat seed from the county station and hybrid maize seed for reliable yields. I apply moderate fertilizer in line with local practice — compound basal plus urea topdress — and use my well irrigation for 4 targeted applications on wheat and 2 on maize, supplementing summer rains. Rotary tillage prepares the seedbed before wheat, while maize goes in no-till straight after wheat harvest to save time and keep the ground from drying out. With some off-farm income in the household I can afford proper inputs, but I stick to what I know works rather than taking risks.
